title: He Traveled 5× Farther Than Marco Polo

lines: You were taught that Marco Polo was the great traveller of the Middle Ages.
This man went almost five times farther.
About one hundred seventeen thousand kilometres, by the best estimate. Yet most people have never heard his name.
His name was Ibn Battuta. He left Tangier, in Morocco, for one pilgrimage, and came back twenty-four years later.
So, three questions. How did a man with almost no money pay for a journey like that? What nearly killed him, again and again?
And if he went that far, why did Europe forget him for almost five hundred years? By the end, you will see his whole route on one map.
This is the journey of Ibn Battuta.
First, where are we? Tangier sits at the very tip of North Africa, where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic.
He was born here in thirteen hundred four, into a family of Muslim judges, and he studied Islamic law.
On the fourteenth of June, thirteen twenty-five, aged about twenty-one, he set out alone. No caravan, no companion.
His goal was Mecca, for the Hajj, the pilgrimage every Muslim should make once. The trip there and back usually took about sixteen months.
He later wrote that leaving his parents felt like a bird leaving its nest. He would not see Morocco again for twenty-four years.
He followed the coast east, through Tlemcen and Bejaia, in today's Algeria, to Tunis, in today's Tunisia.
So far, a young scholar has left home alone. But how does a man with almost nothing pay his way across a continent?
Along the way he joined caravans, long lines of travellers and camels moving together, because alone, a traveller was easy prey for robbers.
But he had a secret weapon. He was trained in Islamic law, and in his world, a learned man was welcome almost anywhere Muslims ruled.
From Morocco to India, rulers and scholars gave guests like him food, a bed, gifts, and sometimes a job.
So for much of his journey, Ibn Battuta did not pay his own way. He travelled on hospitality, from one city to the next.
After more than three thousand five hundred kilometres he reached Alexandria, then Cairo, the capital of the Mamluk sultans who ruled Egypt and Syria.
From there he went north to Jerusalem and Damascus, in today's Syria, and joined the great pilgrim caravan heading south across the desert.
About thirteen hundred kilometres later he reached Medina, and then Mecca. It was November, thirteen twenty-six. His first Hajj was done.
Any other pilgrim would now go home. Ibn Battuta did not.
So far, his learning paid his way, and Mecca was only the first stop. Next, he turned toward Iraq and Persia.
He crossed the desert to Najaf and Basra, in today's Iraq, then went east into Persia, to Isfahan and Shiraz, in today's Iran.
In Baghdad he found a city still partly in ruins, almost seventy years after the Mongols had sacked it.
He went back to Mecca and stayed there for a while to study. Then he chose the sea.
From Jeddah he sailed down the Red Sea to Aden, in Yemen, and on along the coast of East Africa.
Mogadishu, in today's Somalia. Mombasa, in Kenya. And then Kilwa, in Tanzania, a port that grew rich on the gold trade.
He called Kilwa one of the finest and most beautifully built towns he had seen.
And here is a strange thought. By our rough estimate, somewhere on these seas he had already travelled as far as Marco Polo's entire journey.
He was about twenty-five years old. And he was only getting started.
So far: Iraq, Persia, and Africa's east coast. Now he wanted to work for the richest ruler he had heard of: the Sultan of Delhi.
But he did not take the short way. He went through Anatolia, today's Türkiye, and crossed the Black Sea from Sinop.
On the other side lay the Golden Horde, a Mongol state that ruled the steppe, the endless grassland north of the Black Sea.
He joined the moving camp of its khan, Özbeg, a whole city of tents and wagons rolling across the grass.
He also says he went north up the Volga, to a town called Bulgar. Many historians doubt that trip ever happened.
Then came a surprise. One of the khan's wives, Bayalun, was a Byzantine princess. She was pregnant, and wanted to give birth at home, in Constantinople.
Ibn Battuta went with her. A Muslim judge from Morocco walked through the Christian capital, today's Istanbul, and visited the great church of Hagia Sophia.
Then he turned east, across today's Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, to the great cities of Bukhara and Samarkand.
He crossed the Hindu Kush mountains, and in thirteen thirty-three he reached the Indus River, the gateway to India.
Delhi was ruled by Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq. He was clever, very generous, and one of the most frightening men of his age.
He gave Ibn Battuta a big salary and a job as a qadi, a judge, in Delhi.
But the sultan was also brutally violent. He punished fast and killed easily, and no one at his court ever felt safe.
Ibn Battuta stayed about seven years. Then he visited a holy man the sultan distrusted.
That was enough. He was put under guard for nine days, and he believed he would be executed.
He survived. He gave away what he owned and lived for five months as a hermit outside Delhi.
Then the sultan called him back, and offered him a job most men would kill for: ambassador to the Emperor of China.
So far: Delhi made him rich, and nearly got him killed. And the trip to China would go wrong even faster.
In thirteen forty-one the embassy set out with gifts for China. On the way to the coast, rebels attacked. He was robbed, captured, and barely escaped.
He caught up with the others and travelled to Calicut, today's Kozhikode, on India's west coast, where the ships for China waited.
Then a storm hit the harbour. He was still on shore when one of the ships was smashed, and many people on board drowned.
The other ship sailed away with his belongings. In one night he lost the embassy, the gifts, and his job.
He was afraid to face the sultan. So he sailed to the Maldives, a chain of tiny islands in the Indian Ocean.
There, a man who had lost everything became chief judge again. He married several times, and into the royal family.
He visited Ceylon, today's Sri Lanka, and climbed its holy mountain. But on the next voyage, pirates took almost everything he had left.
So far: robbed twice, nearly drowned, and nothing left. Any sensible man would go home. Instead, he sailed for China.
From Chittagong, in today's Bangladesh, he sailed to Sumatra, in Indonesia, and on to Quanzhou, a huge port on the coast of China.
He describes Chinese silk and porcelain, paper money instead of coins, and Muslim merchants with their own mosques.
But here, historians start to doubt him. His China is vaguer than the rest of the book, and he gets some things wrong.
He says he reached Beijing, the Mongol capital. Many scholars think he never got that far, and borrowed some details from other writers.
Remember, he told this story from memory, years later, without notes. So treat the China part with care. Much of the rest fits other sources.
So far: China is the shakiest part of his story. And on the way home, he sailed straight into the Black Death.
He sailed back west, past India and Arabia. In Syria he learned that his father had died fifteen years earlier.
Then, in thirteen forty-eight, the Black Death reached the cities he was passing through, a plague that killed people within days.
In Damascus, his book says, about two thousand four hundred people were dying every day. Cairo was hit just as hard.
He kept going. He made one last Hajj in Mecca, then took the long road west, toward home.
In thirteen forty-nine he reached Morocco. Only then did he learn that his mother had died, just months before he arrived.
He visited her grave in Tangier. Then he settled in Fez, the sultan's capital. He was about forty-five years old.
So far: twenty-four years on the road, and he was still not done. One great Muslim kingdom was missing from his list.
South of Morocco lies the Sahara. Beyond it was the Empire of Mali, famous all over the world for its gold.
This map was drawn in Spain around thirteen seventy-five. It shows a king of Mali on his throne, holding a huge piece of gold.
In thirteen fifty-two he crossed the Sahara with a camel caravan. At Taghaza, even the houses were built from slabs of salt.
He reached the capital of Mali and met its king, Mansa Sulayman, the brother of the famous Mansa Musa.
He was not impressed. The king's welcome gift, he complained, was three loaves of bread, some fried beef, and a gourd of yogurt.
He also saw Timbuktu, on the Niger River. Then he crossed the desert north again, and was home by early thirteen fifty-four.
So far: his travelling days were over. But his story still had to make its own journey.
In Fez, Sultan Abu Inan asked him to tell his story to a young court writer, Ibn Juzayy.
Ibn Battuta talked, and Ibn Juzayy wrote and polished. Around thirteen fifty-five the book was finished: the Rihla, which simply means the journey.
So why did Europe forget him? Because Europe never really knew him. The book was in Arabic, and its copies stayed in the Muslim world.
Marco Polo's book spread across Europe in many languages, and it inspired Christopher Columbus.
Europeans only discovered Ibn Battuta in the nineteenth century. The full text with a French translation came out between eighteen fifty-three and eighteen fifty-eight.
So, the answers. He paid his way with his learning and other people's hospitality. He survived bandits, a tyrant, a shipwreck, pirates and the plague.
Here is Marco Polo's journey. And here is Ibn Battuta's: about one hundred seventeen thousand kilometres, and at least forty of today's countries.
Historians still argue about some of his stops. But even the parts they trust make him one of the greatest travellers who ever lived.
So who should we really call the great traveller of the Middle Ages? Tell me in the comments.
On his very first road, he passed Tunis, right next to the ruins of ancient Carthage. Why Rome destroyed it is right here on screen.
Thanks for watching.
